analysis.one_liner: Diverts payroll tax into personal investment accounts while raising Social Security's full retirement age to 70.
analysis.headline: Referred to two House committees on October 13, 1998, the bill died 82 days later when the 105th Congress ended, without a hearing, a vote, or backing beyond one Democratic cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would take two percentage points of the Social Security payroll tax that workers now pay (6.2% dropping to 4.2%) and put it instead into a personal "individual security account" for each worker, topped up by up to $2,000 a year of optional contributions. To pay for it and extend solvency, it would raise the full retirement age to 70 and the early retirement age to 65, cut spousal benefits from 50% to 33%, trim the benefit formula and future cost-of-living raises, and phase out a transfer from Social Security to Medicare's hospital fund. It would pair those cuts with a new minimum benefit near the poverty line for long-term low earners and an end to the rule that reduces benefits for people who keep working past retirement age.
analysis.who_benefits: The financial services industry would gain an enormous new pool of retirement money to manage: every worker's diverted payroll contribution would flow into an individual account, and the bill orders the fund's board to study and recommend ways to expand investment options and rollovers — the entry point for private fund management, since the accounts would initially sit in a low-fee government-run fund modeled on the federal Thrift Savings Plan [S2][S3]. Workers born after 1944 would own the accounts and could benefit from market returns [S3]. Higher earners who work past retirement age would gain from repealing the earnings test [S2][S3]. Long-term low-wage workers would gain a new minimum benefit pegged toward the poverty line starting with those qualifying after 2005 [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fund managers, higher earners, low-wage retirees

how_it_helps.text: Channels two percentage points of every covered worker's payroll tax into an individually owned retirement account, plus up to $2,000 a year in additional optional contributions, giving workers assets that are theirs by name and inheritable in a lump sum if they die before drawing them [S3].

Directs the new Individual Security Fund Board to study and report to the President and Congress on ways to increase account holders' investment options, especially for rollovers and distributions — the mechanism by which private fund managers would gain access to the account balances [S2][S3].
Repeals the earnings test, so beneficiaries at or above retirement age could earn any amount from work without losing benefits — a change worth the most to higher earners who keep working [S2][S3].
Creates a new minimum monthly benefit, phased in through a table reaching 60 percent of a poverty-level amount, for long-term low earners who first qualify after 2005 [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Future retirees would pay through a normal retirement age rising to 70 by 2037 (and beyond), an early retirement age rising to 65, spousal benefits cut from 50% to 33% of the worker's benefit, a benefit formula that eventually averages in every working year including low-earning ones, and cost-of-living adjustments reduced by a modified inflation index — changes that fall hardest on people in physically demanding jobs who cannot work longer, and on spouses (often women) with short work records [S2][S3]. The Medicare Hospital Insurance trust fund would also lose a decades-old transfer from Social Security, phased out after 2009 [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Future retirees facing later retirement, smaller checks

drawbacks.text: The full retirement age would climb to 70 by 2037 and the early retirement age to 65, with further increases after 2029 — a worker retiring before the new full age would take a much larger permanent reduction, and people in physically demanding jobs would have the least ability to keep working [S2][S3].

Spousal benefits other than survivor's benefits would be phased down from 50% to 33% of the worker's benefit, cutting incomes mainly for spouses with limited earnings histories, most often women [S2][S3].

Benefits would be computed over more working years (eventually all of them, including low-earning years) and indexed to a modified Consumer Price Index designed to grow more slowly, trimming every future check and compounding over a retirement that could last decades [S2][S3].
The bill phases out the transfer from Social Security to the Medicare Hospital Insurance trust fund after 2009, worsening Medicare's hospital financing while Social Security's books improve [S2][S3].

Its solvency mechanism (Section 13) would create a fast-track procedure — committee discharge, limits on debate, and no amendments — for presidentially endorsed packages of benefit cuts or tax increases, skirting the normal legislative process [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill had real attractions: a poverty-level minimum benefit for career low earners, an end to the earnings test, and personal accounts workers would own and could pass on. But these sat on top of the largest benefit cuts ever proposed in a single Social Security bill to that point: a retirement age of 70, spousal benefits cut by a third, a benefit formula and inflation index that would trim every check, and Medicare financing quietly weakened to help Social Security's ledgers. The accounts were funded by taking money out of the guaranteed benefit system, not adding to it, so workers traded a predictable, inflation-protected benefit for market risk — and the bill was designed so the asset-management industry would eventually administer the money. For someone who could not work past 62 or 65, the losses clearly outweighed the gains.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with just over two months left in the Congress, it was sent to the Ways and Means and Rules committees, which never held a hearing or a vote, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Jim Kolbe introduced the bill on October 13, 1998, joined by Democratic Representative Charles Stenholm, its only cosponsor [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and, for parts within its jurisdiction, to the Rules Committee [S1][S5].
No hearing, markup, or vote is recorded in the bill's action history; the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill expired in committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers who would have faced a retirement age of 70, spousal benefit cuts, and smaller cost-of-living raises kept the existing system, and the financial services industry did not get the new account business. Nobody who supported the reform got anything, because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers who would have faced the cuts

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — a Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor — but it never reached a vote, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.note: Every worker's diverted two-point payroll contribution would flow into an individual account, building a vast new pool of retirement assets. The accounts would initially sit in a low-fee, government-run fund modeled on the Thrift Savings Plan, but the bill orders its board to study expanding investment options and rollovers — the door through which private fund management would eventually enter.

Newly hired state and local employees would be brought under Social Security coverage, requiring payroll contributions from governments that were previously exempt. Workers would gain coverage; their governments would bear a new cost.

The bill phases out, after 2009, the decades-old transfer from Social Security's trust fund to Medicare's Hospital Insurance fund, worsening the financing of the program that pays hospitals for seniors' care.
